item.content:encoded:
News / Crypto Briefing / Bitcoin slides to $62,000 as analysts eye $60,000 as the line in the sand

Bitcoin slides to $62,000 as analysts eye $60,000 as the line in the sand 2 min read

BTCUSD Bitcoin fell to roughly $62,000 on November 15, 2026, its weakest level since July. That leaves the world's largest crypto asset sitting about 50% below its all-time high of approximately $126,000, set in October 2025. According to Forbes, analysts are warning that a break below $60,000 could open the door to a slide under $40,000. That is a conditional forecast, not a done deal. The latest leg down came fast. Bitcoin had peaked at $87,364 on September 21, 2026, according to the research data. Forbes described that September high as nearly $90,000. Either way, the round trip from there to $62,000 works out to a decline of about 29%. Forbes put it at almost 30%. Leverage made it worse. Around $2 billion in positions were liquidated within a single 24-hour window after the drop. Most of those were long positions. Institutional money was also heading for the exits. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded net outflows of more than $1.9 billion in the week leading up to November 13, 2026. The damage shows up clearly in market capitalization. At the lows, Bitcoin's total value sat at approximately $1.3 trillion, down from peaks above $2.5 trillion. That drop also pushed Bitcoin out of the top tier of global asset rankings. Crypto didn't fall in a vacuum. The selloff lined up with US Treasury yields climbing above 5%, a stronger dollar, and continued weakness in AI-related stocks. Then there's Elon Musk. His earlier warnings about a potential US fiscal crisis, tied to national debt surpassing $40 trillion, resurfaced in market chatter around the selloff. Forbes framed it as Musk's "global bankruptcy" scenario suddenly feeling less hypothetical. There's an irony here worth noting. Bitcoin's long-running pitch is that it serves as a hedge against exactly this kind of government debt spiral. Yet when debt fears flared, Bitcoin traded like a tech stock with a hangover rather than a lifeboat. The low near $62,000 is the weakest print since July 2026. The October 2025 peak was built partly on spot ETF demand and the idea that Wall Street had finally embraced the asset. The current slide shows the flip side: the same plumbing that brought money in can move it out just as efficiently. The immediate focus is the $60,000 level. If price breaks through, the analysts cited by Forbes see a path toward the sub-$40,000 range. ETF flows are another key signal. A week of outflows above $1.9 billion reflects institutional caution. Bitcoin is behaving like a risk asset tied to interest rates and tech sentiment, not like a standalone hedge. The next few weeks of Treasury yields, ETF flows, and price action around that key level will likely decide which story wins.

item.content:encoded:
News / Cointelegraph / BTC price tags 18-week low into Nvidia earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week

BTC price tags 18-week low into Nvidia earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week 3 min read

BTCUSD USDJPY Bitcoin BTCUSD traded around $64,500 early Monday after a sell-off in thin weekend trading sent it to a four-month low of $61,950. Key points: Bitcoin fell below its 200-week simple moving average, now at $68,186. Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings Tuesday following Jensen Huang’s resignation, with the company forecasting about $108 billion in revenue. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks Monday, and minutes of the Fed’s October policy meeting are due Wednesday. Bitcoin falls below its 200-week moving average Data from TradingView showed that BTCUSD fell to $61,950 on Bitstamp, a level last seen on July 13. The pair briefly rebounded to $66,000 before easing to around $64,500 during Monday’s Asian trading session.

BTCUSD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView The drop pushed Bitcoin below its 200-week simple moving average (SMA) of $68,186. This cemented concerns about Bitcoin’s rebound to $87,000, which began in August, as flipping the 200-week SMA from resistance to support has been a prerequisite for previous bear-market recoveries. “Deviating below the 200-week SMA has historically been the key to building out a Bear Market bottom formation,” crypto trader and analyst Rekt Capital said Saturday on X.

BTCUSD one-week chart with 200-week SMA. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView From Friday to 10 am UTC on Monday, Bitcoin open interest fell by around 9.1% to $20.98 billion, according to onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant. A CryptoQuant contributing analyst drew comparisons to similar open interest drawdowns in February and June, considering whether Bitcoin was forming a local bottom. “If the flush is complete, a bottoming zone may be near. If shorts keep piling up, even a modest rally could squeeze them. The $59K-$60K summer low remains the next key test,” the analyst wrote on Sunday.

Bitcoin open interest. Source: CryptoQuant Bitcoin perpetual futures funding rates briefly turned negative near the weekend low, meaning traders with short positions paid those with long positions.

Bitcoin funding rates. Source: CryptoQuant Nvidia earnings due Tuesday as allies push for Huang’s return Nvidia remains in the spotlight this week as the tech giant reports third-quarter results after US markets close Tuesday amid ongoing controversy over former CEO Jensen Huang. On Tuesday, interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the company’s earnings call. Nvidia previously forecast quarterly revenue of around $108 billion, and analysts expect earnings per share to nearly double year over year. Huang is reportedly considering a return to Nvidia. He resigned last week after reports that he had an affair with a chip executive whom US authorities suspect of spying for China. Beijing denied the espionage allegation. The Financial Times reported that a “war room” of tech CEOs and others was lobbying for his reinstatement, while an open letter calling for his return has garnered more than 165,000 signatories, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk said in an X post on Friday. The efforts face friction from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said that Nvidia should hire its next CEO from outside the company. “This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader that they need to go outside the company, that just [with] what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shakeup,” he told Fox News. Nvidia shares closed Friday at $162.85, down 12.7% for the week. On Thursday, shares fell to $148.80, their lowest since mid-2025, before recovering some of their losses.

Nvidia stock one-week chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView Nvidia headlines rattled tech stocks and crypto markets last week. Investors will be watching the company’s outlook for signs of how demand for AI chips is holding up. Fed minutes due as markets price in December rate hike Fed officials will speak throughout the week as traders look for clues about the December rate decision. Warsh will deliver opening remarks at the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco at 9 am PT (5 pm UTC) on Monday. He will also moderate two panels and a fireside chat. On Wednesday, the Fed will release minutes of its Oct. 27–28 policy meeting. Officials left rates unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, and Warsh cited “resilient” domestic spending in the face of global geopolitical uncertainty. After the latest economic data, markets fully priced in a quarter-point rate hike from the Fed in December. Last week’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) beat expectations, and while the Producer Price Index (PPI) reading was lower than anticipated, the annual increase was still the largest in four years. Meanwhile, the 10-year US Treasury yield rose above 5%, and the Japanese yen brought back a familiar headwind for crypto markets as it weakened past the key psychological level of 160 per US dollar on Friday.

USDJPY one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView Japan’s economy shrank at an annualized rate of 0.1% in the third quarter, according to data released Monday. The contraction complicates the outlook for further rate hikes in Japan, where the policy rate is already at a three-decade high of 1.25%. “With the yen perched precariously at 160 per dollar, a combination of sluggish domestic growth and sticky price pressures, if they were to materialize, would complicate life for both the Bank of Japan and the Ministry of Finance,” economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote over the weekend.
